claim: The murine first upper molar shows repeated anterior elongation at different scales, from the intra-population to the interspecific level.
source: At different scales, from the intra-population to the interspecific, the murine first upper molar shows repeated anterior elongation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key observation about morphological variation in murine molars.

claim: DUHi and FVB mouse strains differ in temporal, spatial and functional aspects of tooth signaling center activity.
source: Using a novel quantitative approach to compare the development of two mouse strains with short or long molars, we identified temporal, spatial and functional differences in tooth signaling center activity, that arise from differential tuning of the activation-inhibition mechanisms underlying tooth patterning.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that temporal, spatial and functional differences were identified through quantitative comparison.

claim: The differences in tooth signaling center activity between DUHi and FVB strains arise from differential tuning of activation-inhibition mechanisms underlying tooth patterning.
source: Using a novel quantitative approach to compare the development of two mouse strains with short or long molars, we identified temporal, spatial and functional differences in tooth signaling center activity, that arise from differential tuning of the activation-inhibition mechanisms underlying tooth patterning.
evidence: The abstract explicitly attributes the observed differences to differential tuning of activation-inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Only the upper first molar reacts to developmental differences via elongation of its anterior part.
source: By tracing their fate, we could explain why only the upper first molar reacts via elongation of its anterior part.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from fate tracing experiments.

claim: Individuals of the elongated DUHi strain varied in tooth length despite a lack of genetic variation.
source: Despite a lack of genetic variation, individuals of the elongated strain varied in tooth length and the temporal dynamics of their signaling centers, highlighting the intrinsic instability of the upper molar developmental system.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that variation exists despite lack of genetic variation in the inbred strain.

claim: Individuals of the elongated DUHi strain varied in the temporal dynamics of their signaling centers.
source: Despite a lack of genetic variation, individuals of the elongated strain varied in tooth length and the temporal dynamics of their signaling centers, highlighting the intrinsic instability of the upper molar developmental system.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that temporal dynamics of signaling centers varied between individuals.

claim: The upper molar developmental system is intrinsically unstable.
source: Despite a lack of genetic variation, individuals of the elongated strain varied in tooth length and the temporal dynamics of their signaling centers, highlighting the intrinsic instability of the upper molar developmental system.
evidence: The abstract explicitly characterizes the upper molar developmental system as intrinsically unstable based on observed variation.

claim: The variational properties of murine molar development drive morphological evolution along a line of least resistance.
source: Collectively, these results reveal the variational properties of murine molar development that drive morphological evolution along a line of least resistance.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this interpretation of the collective results.

claim: Developmental mechanisms can confer specific variational properties on a trait and thereby channel its evolutionary trajectory.
source: Evolutionary developmental biology postulates that developmental mechanisms confer specific variational properties on a trait, and can thereby channel its evolutionary trajectory.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate of evolutionary developmental biology in the introduction.

claim: The main direction of phenotypic variation in first molar shape in murine rodents divides species with narrower molars from species with broader molars.
source: In this group, the main direction of phenotypic variation in first molar shape divides species with narrower molars (with narrower cusps, for example dwarf mice of Nannomys subgenus in Figure 1) from species with broader molars (with broader, more roundish cusps, e.g. wood mice or grass mice of Arvicanthis genus, Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Narrow teeth are mostly found in faunivorous rodents while broad teeth are characteristics of herbivorous ones.
source: These differences in tooth morphology have been associated with different diet preferences, narrow teeth being mostly found in faunivorous rodents while broad teeth are characteristics of herbivorous ones, because of the latter allowing the consumption of harder and more abrasive food (Gómez Cano et al., 2013).
evidence: This association is stated with a citation to support it.

claim: Broad teeth allow the consumption of harder and more abrasive food.
source: These differences in tooth morphology have been associated with different diet preferences, narrow teeth being mostly found in faunivorous rodents while broad teeth are characteristics of herbivorous ones, because of the latter allowing the consumption of harder and more abrasive food (Gómez Cano et al., 2013).
evidence: This functional explanation is provided with a citation.

claim: Molar tooth morphology reflects adaptation in murine rodents.
source: Molar tooth morphology thus reflects adaptation in murine rodents as seen in many other mammals.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the diet-morphology associations.

claim: Variation within a taxon reproduces the basic variation ranging from narrow to broad tooth, regardless of the mean morphology of the taxon.
source: However, whatever the mean morphology of a taxon, the variation within a taxon (e.g. house mouse and wood mouse), including at the population level, seems to reproduce, to a lesser degree, the basic variation ranging from narrow to broad tooth (Renaud et al., 2009; Renaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This pattern is stated with citations to support it.

claim: Micro-scale variation in tooth morphology is more likely to be shaped by developmental properties rather than adaptation.
source: Such micro-scale variation is more likely to be shaped by developmental properties, rather than adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the nature of within-taxon variation.

claim: The high integration between the variation of lower and upper first molars suggests that both evolved in a concerted manner under similar developmental constraints.
source: The high integration between the variation of lower and upper first molars suggests that both evolved in a concerted manner under similar developmental constraints.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observed integration.

claim: In some species or populations, only the upper molar tends to elongate, specifically from its anterior part which may even form an additional small cusp.
source: On top of that, in some species or populations, only the upper molar tends to elongate, specifically from its anterior part which may even form an additional small cusp (Misonne, 1969; Renaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This pattern is stated with citations to support it.

claim: The additional anteriormost cusp is especially common in the Mus genus.
source: This additional cusp is especially common in the Mus genus (yet occasionally seen in other murine species Misonne, 1969).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support it.

claim: The additional anteriormost cusp is especially marked in some species of the Mus (Nannomys) subgenus.
source: For example, it is especially marked in some species of the Mus (Nannomys) subgenus, and also repeatedly seen in diverse house mouse populations (Renaud et al., 2011, see later Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and referenced to Figure 1.

claim: Anterior elongation of the upper molar evolved independently in many Mus (Mus) musculus domesticus island populations.
source: In particular, it evolved independently in many Mus (Mus) musculus domesticus island populations (e.g. on several Corsican islands, Marion Island [Renaud et al., 2011], Orkney islands [Ledevin et al., 2016; Renaud et al., 2018], as well as on Kerguelen and the Canary islands, S. Renaud, [Ledevin et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting independent evolution in different populations.

claim: Anterior elongation is found associated with increased body size in domestic mouse populations.
source: Interestingly, anterior elongation is found associated with increased body size in domestic mouse populations (Renaud et al., 2011), being trapped on island (and following 'Foster's rule', or 'island rule' where small mammals become gigantic) or in cold environments.
evidence: This association is stated with a citation to support it.

claim: During molar development, signaling centers called 'enamel knots' are positioned in the epithelium by activation-inhibition mechanisms.
source: During molar development, signaling centers, called 'enamel knots', are positioned in the epithelium by activation-inhibition mechanisms, and determine the location where the crown, or later the cusps, form Jernvall et al. (1994); Sadier et al. (2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Enamel knots determine the location where the crown, or later the cusps, form.
source: During molar development, signaling centers, called 'enamel knots', are positioned in the epithelium by activation-inhibition mechanisms, and determine the location where the crown, or later the cusps, form Jernvall et al. (1994); Sadier et al. (2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Structures found transiently in mouse embryos are thought to correspond to premolar rudiments.
source: Although murine rodents lack premolar teeth, structures found transiently in mouse embryos are thought to correspond to their rudiments, each with their own signaling centers, notably secreting the signaling molecule Shh (Lesot et al., 1998; Peterková et al., 1996; Prochazka et al., 2010; Viriot et al., 2000; Peterková et al., 2002).
evidence: This interpretation is stated with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: Following molar row initiation around 11.5 dpc, the dental epithelium progressively invaginates into the mesenchyme along the antero-posterior jaw axis.
source: Following molar row initiation around 11.5 dpc, the dental epithelium progressively invaginates into the mesenchyme along the antero-posterior jaw axis, and Shh-signaling centers are patterned sequentially in this epithelial ridge (Prochazka et al., 2010; Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This developmental sequence is stated with citations.

claim: Shh-signaling centers are patterned sequentially in the epithelial ridge.
source: Following molar row initiation around 11.5 dpc, the dental epithelium progressively invaginates into the mesenchyme along the antero-posterior jaw axis, and Shh-signaling centers are patterned sequentially in this epithelial ridge (Prochazka et al., 2010; Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This developmental pattern is stated with citations.

claim: In the mandible, the first and most anterior signaling center has formed by 12.5 dpc but disappears soon after in CD1 mice.
source: In mandible, the first and most anterior signaling center, associated with a discrete epithelial swelling, has formed by 12.5 dpc but disappears soon after (in CD1 mice).
evidence: This timing is stated for CD1 mice specifically.

claim: A second signaling center (R2 signaling center) has formed more posteriorly by 13.5 dpc.
source: A second signaling center (R2 signaling center) has formed more posteriorly by 13.5 dpc, where the epithelial ridge locally enlarges and gives rise to a more prominent bud called R2.
evidence: This timing and location are stated as established knowledge.

claim: The R2 structure was interpreted as a rudiment of a suppressed premolar.
source: This structure was interpreted as a rudiment of a suppressed premolar (Prochazka et al., 2010; Viriot et al., 2000), and can form a small tooth in mutant conditions interpreted as an atavistic premolar (Cobourne and Sharpe, 2010; Lagronova-Churava et al., 2013; Lochovska et al., 2015; Peterková et al., 2005).
evidence: This interpretation is stated with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: R2 can form a small tooth in mutant conditions interpreted as an atavistic premolar.
source: This structure was interpreted as a rudiment of a suppressed premolar (Prochazka et al., 2010; Viriot et al., 2000), and can form a small tooth in mutant conditions interpreted as an atavistic premolar (Cobourne and Sharpe, 2010; Lagronova-Churava et al., 2013; Lochovska et al., 2015; Peterková et al., 2005).
evidence: This observation is stated with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: By 14.0 dpc, a third, even more posterior, signaling center has formed, called the early M1 signaling center.
source: This signaling center also soon vanishes and by 14.0 dpc, a third, even more posterior, signaling center has formed, called the early M1 signaling center.
evidence: This timing is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the lower jaw, the R2 signaling center interacts in a complex manner with the signaling center of the first molar.
source: In the lower jaw, the R2 signaling center interacts in a complex manner with the signaling center of the first molar.
evidence: This interaction is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the lower jaw, R2 and M1 signaling centers transiently co-exist before fusing to form the mature M1 signaling center known as the pEK.
source: Both transiently co-exist before fusing to form the mature M1 signaling center known as the pEK (Lochovska et al., 2015; Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This developmental sequence is stated with citations.

claim: The pEK drives 'cap transition', a morphogenetic transition during which the epithelium starts to fold around the mesenchyme to form the tooth crown.
source: This pEK drives 'cap transition', a morphogenetic transition during which the epithelium starts to fold around the mesenchyme to form the tooth crown.
evidence: This function of the pEK is stated as established knowledge.

claim: From an early cap stage, the R2 primordium becomes integrated into the anterior part of the first lower first molar.
source: From an early cap stage, the R2 primordium becomes thus integrated into the anterior part of the first lower first molar.
evidence: This integration is stated as established knowledge.

claim: A similar R2 bud is present in the upper jaw.
source: Although a similar R2 bud is also present in the upper jaw (Lesot et al., 1998; Peterková et al., 1996), its developmental relationship to the upper first molar is less clear.
evidence: This presence is stated with citations.

claim: The upper R2 bud is not incorporated during the initial stage of molar cap development, unlike its lower counterpart.
source: It is not incorporated during the initial stage of molar cap development, as seen for its lower counterpart (Peterkova et al., 2006).
evidence: This difference is stated with a citation.

claim: The distance between R2 and M1 signaling centers is larger in the upper jaw.
source: Recently, we have shown that the distance between R2 and M1 signaling centers is larger in the upper jaw, where the two signaling centers do not fuse at the cap stage (Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This finding is stated with a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: In the upper jaw, R2 and M1 signaling centers do not fuse at the cap stage.
source: Recently, we have shown that the distance between R2 and M1 signaling centers is larger in the upper jaw, where the two signaling centers do not fuse at the cap stage (Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This finding is stated with a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The DUHi mice display narrow molars with elongated first upper molars, and an additional cusp in some individuals.
source: In our effort to test the correlation between this morphology and a large body size, we found that the DUHi mice, an inbred strain that was established following artificial selection for increased body size (Bünger and Herrendörfer, 1994; Bünger et al., 1982), display narrow molars with elongated first upper molars, and an additional cusp in some individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FVB mice display wide molars with short first upper molars.
source: In contrast, the FVB mice, an inbred strain often used to maintain genetic modifications, display wide molars with short first upper molars (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first axis of the PCA contrasts broad with narrow outlines for both the upper and lower molar.
source: For both the upper and lower molar, the first axis of the PCA contrasts broad with narrow outlines.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The variation in outline is more pronounced for the upper molar (PCA UM1 = 62%) than for the lower molar (PC1 LM1 = 46% of variance).
source: However, this variation is more pronounced for the upper molar (PCA UM1 = 62% instead of PC1 LM1 = 46% of variance) because it also involves a change focused at the anterior part of the tooth, and opposing short vs. anteriorly elongated UM1.
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The variation in the upper molar involves a change focused at the anterior part of the tooth, opposing short vs. anteriorly elongated UM1.
source: However, this variation is more pronounced for the upper molar (PCA UM1 = 62% instead of PC1 LM1 = 46% of variance) because it also involves a change focused at the anterior part of the tooth, and opposing short vs. anteriorly elongated UM1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Anterior elongation occurs in otherwise narrow molars, while broad molars have a short anterior part.
source: We note that although the PCA of the outline descriptors could in principle separate these two types of variation, this was not the case, showing that these two types of variation are correlated in the upper molar (i.e. anterior elongation occurs in otherwise narrow molars, while broad molars have a short anterior part).
evidence: This correlation is stated as an inference from the PCA results.

claim: The direction of variation between FVB and DUHi strains recapitulates the direction of variation seen in murine rodents as a whole.
source: The position of FVB and DUHi strains along the PC1 axis and length/width ratio indicate that the direction of variation between the two strains recapitulates the direction of variation seen in murine rodents as a whole (e.g. broader FVB molars versus narrower DUHi molars, lower and upper M1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The variation between FVB and DUHi strains recapitulates the variation specifically seen in the upper first molars of the Mus genus.
source: Moreover, it recapitulates the variation specifically seen in the upper first molars of the Mus genus (short FVB versus anteriorly elongated DUHi upper molars, with additional cusp).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: DUHi teeth fall with the most elongated upper molars among wild Mus musculus domesticus samples.
source: Indeed, the two strains are representative of extreme wild Mus musculus domesticus samples: DUHi teeth fall with the most elongated upper molars (e.g. samples from a very small Corsican island: Piana), while the FVB upper molars fall with the most 'short and wide' upper molars (e.g. samples from the continent (Gardouch locality) or from a large Orkney island: Eday).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: FVB upper molars fall with the most 'short and wide' upper molars among wild Mus musculus domesticus samples.
source: Indeed, the two strains are representative of extreme wild Mus musculus domesticus samples: DUHi teeth fall with the most elongated upper molars (e.g. samples from a very small Corsican island: Piana), while the FVB upper molars fall with the most 'short and wide' upper molars (e.g. samples from the continent (Gardouch locality) or from a large Orkney island: Eday).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neither the age in days post-coïtum nor the embryonic body weight solely provide a correct estimation of embryonic age.
source: In order to allow the developmental trajectories of the developing molar teeth to be compared, embryonic samples were taken from a wide developmental window in the two strains in question (12.0 to 15.5 dpc). For each strain, multiple litters were sampled every half day, ensuring even coverage due to the slight variation in developmental stage within litters. Taking account of the dynamic nature of the system required a numeric estimation of the embryonic age of embryos (i.e. an age reflecting the progress in embryogenesis). Neither the age in days post-coïtum nor the embryonic body weight solely provide a correct estimation (for further explanation, see Materials and methods and Appendix 1).
evidence: This limitation is stated and explained in the text.

claim: A Bayesian modeling approach was devised to compute a strain-specific embryonic age for each embryo by combining age in days post-coïtum and embryonic body weight.
source: Therefore, in this study, we devised a Bayesian modeling approach to compute a strain-specific embryonic age for each embryo (later called cdpc) by combining these two information (see Materials and methods and Appendix 1 for further precisions).
evidence: This methodological approach is explicitly described.

claim: The Bayesian model does not correct for developmental stage differences between strains, but reveals them by providing a time framework.
source: Because the model does not comprise information on actual stage differences and we estimate cdpc for each strain, it will not correct for developmental stages differences between strains, but instead reveal them by providing a time framework, the computed age (e.g. cap transition occurs at earlier cdpc in FVB).
evidence: This property of the model is explicitly stated.

claim: In both strains, Shh expression is seen at the signaling center of the R2 bud.
source: In both jaws and strains, we see Shh expression at the signaling center of the R2 bud (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shh expression at R2 fades away as development proceeds.
source: This expression then fades away (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 E-H).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: A second spot of Shh expression appears, which represents the early M1 signaling center.
source: A second spot of expression appears, which represents the early M1 signaling center (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: As development proceeds to the cap transition stage, the M1 expression zone increases in size to form a 'mature M1 signaling center'.
source: As development proceeds to the cap transition stage, the M1 expression zone increases in size (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2) to form a 'mature M1 signaling center' (differences between lower and upper jaw in this process will be emphasized later), and the tooth continues to develop (Figure 2—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: In the upper jaw of DUHi mice, the fading R2 spot frequently co-occurs with a distinct M1 spot.
source: In the upper jaw of DUHi mice, we frequently see the co-occurrence of the fading R2 spot with a distinct M1 spot (Figure 2M–T and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2 M-T).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The number of developmental states observed (11 for upper molar, 9 for lower molar) was much smaller than the mathematical maximum theoretically possible (54).
source: Mathematically speaking, this yields 54 possible total states of the dental epithelium, which can be conceptualized as a theoretical 'developmental space' through which each individual will move as it develops. However, not all of this space is occupied; the number of states observed was much smaller than the mathematical maximum theoretically possible (11 states for the upper molar, Figure 3; and 9 states for the lower molar, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The unfolding of normal development imposes rules on characters' state transitions and combinations.
source: This is because the unfolding of normal development imposes rules on characters' state transitions and combinations.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the limited number of observed states.

claim: The actual occupied proportion of developmental space and the trajectories through this space are properties of a given genotype with a given development.
source: This emphasizes that the actual occupied proportion of developmental space and the trajectories through this space are properties of a given genotype with a given development.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the developmental space concept.

claim: Certain developmental states are only present in one of the two strains (3 DUHi-exclusive states, 2 FVB-exclusive states for upper molar).
source: A comparison of the distribution of developmental states seen in DUHi and FVB upper molar samples reveals that certain states are only present in one of these two strains. This is especially true for upper molar (3 DUHi-exclusive states, 2 FVB-exclusive states) as compared with lower molar (1 DUHi-exclusive state, evidenced by only two samples).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Within a given weight range (from 14.25 to 14.75 cdpc; 175 mg to 225 mg), all DUHi samples display a 'DUHi-exclusive' state, while all FVB samples display an 'FVB-exclusive' state.
source: Indeed, within a given weight range (from 14.25 to 14.75 cdpc; 175 mg to 225 mg), all DUHi samples display a 'DUHi-exclusive' state, while all FVB samples display an 'FVB-exclusive' state.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The period of strain-exclusive states corresponds to the period between the disappearance of the R2 signaling center and the maturation of the M1 signaling center.
source: This corresponded to the period between the disappearance of the R2 signaling center and the maturation of the M1 signaling center.
evidence: This temporal correspondence is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The developmental differences between DUHi and FVB strains can be conceived of as each strain following distinct trajectories through 'developmental space'.
source: Therefore, the developmental differences between these two strains can be conceived of as each of the two strains following distinct trajectories through 'developmental space'.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the developmental state data.

claim: The developmental differences between DUHi and FVB strains are especially marked in the upper molar.
source: Moreover, these differences are especially marked in the upper molar.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the comparative observations.

claim: In upper molars, the R2 expression zone persists longer in DUHi than in FVB (logistic regression: p<1.10E-8).
source: In upper molars (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the R2 expression zone persists longer in DUHi than in FVB (logistic regression: presence of R2 signaling center activity in relation to computed embryo age, p<1.10E-8, see Supplementary statistical details 1).
evidence: This statistical finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The R2 and M1 signaling centers frequently co-occur in DUHi upper molars.
source: The R2 and M1 signaling center frequently co-occur in DUHi, and co-occurence of R2 and a mature (large) M1 signaling center was only seen in DUHi upper molars.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Co-occurrence of R2 and a mature (large) M1 signaling center was only seen in DUHi upper molars.
source: The R2 and M1 signaling center frequently co-occur in DUHi, and co-occurence of R2 and a mature (large) M1 signaling center was only seen in DUHi upper molars.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Early M1 signaling center was seen without a R2 signaling center only in FVB mice.
source: In contrast, early M1 signaling center was seen without a R2 signaling center only in FVB mice.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The M1 spot appears later in DUHi than in FVB embryos (logistic regression: p<0.01).
source: A logistic regression also revealed a statistically significant difference in the timing of the appearance of the M1 spot, which appears later in DUHi than in FVB embryos (p<0.01, see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This statistical finding is stated in the text.

claim: The longer persistence of R2 signaling center and later appearance of the early M1 signaling center in the upper jaw of DUHi mice were associated with a more prominent R2 bud.
source: The longer persistence of R2 signaling center and later appearance of the early M1 signaling center in the upper jaw of DUHi mice were associated with a more prominent R2 bud, as seen in dissociated epithelium (Figure 2, Figure 4-F) but also in 3D reconstructions of tooth germs (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This association is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 4.

claim: In the lower jaw, R2 and M1 signaling centers occasionally coexist only in DUHi, but never in FVB.
source: In the lower jaw, we observed a similar tendency, with R2 and M1 signaling centers occasionally coexisting only in DUHi, but never in FVB (Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3.

claim: In both strains, the lower R2 signaling center is ultimately part of the mature M1 signaling center known as the pEK.
source: In both strains, the lower R2 signaling center was ultimately part of the mature M1 signaling center known as the pEK (Figure 2—figure supplement 1R and P), as shown for other mouse strains (Lochovska et al., 2015).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, with a citation to support it.

claim: The M1 signaling center is shifted posteriorly in DUHi mice compared to FVB mice.
source: Our measurements revealed that the M1 signaling center was shifted posteriorly in DUHi mice: the pre-M1 signaling center region was longer in DUHi than in FVB samples (Figure 4H,t-test, p<0.01), while the post-M1 signaling center region was shorter in DUHi upper molars than in FVB (Figure 4I,t-test, p<0.01; see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4, with statistical support.

claim: The pre-M1 signaling center region is longer in DUHi than in FVB upper molar samples (t-test, p<0.01).
source: Our measurements revealed that the M1 signaling center was shifted posteriorly in DUHi mice: the pre-M1 signaling center region was longer in DUHi than in FVB samples (Figure 4H,t-test, p<0.01), while the post-M1 signaling center region was shorter in DUHi upper molars than in FVB (Figure 4I,t-test, p<0.01; see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This measurement is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4, with statistical support.

claim: The post-M1 signaling center region is shorter in DUHi upper molars than in FVB (t-test, p<0.01).
source: Our measurements revealed that the M1 signaling center was shifted posteriorly in DUHi mice: the pre-M1 signaling center region was longer in DUHi than in FVB samples (Figure 4H,t-test, p<0.01), while the post-M1 signaling center region was shorter in DUHi upper molars than in FVB (Figure 4I,t-test, p<0.01; see Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This measurement is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4, with statistical support.

claim: No statistically significant differences in total dental epithelium length were found between DUHi and FVB upper molars.
source: No statistically significant differences in total dental epithelium length was found (Figure 4J).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the case of the lower molars, no statistically significant inter-strain differences in measurements emerged.
source: In the case of the lower molars (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, see Supplementary file 4), no statistically significant inter-strain differences emerged.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The posterior growth rate is unchanged between the two strains.
source: This finding suggests that the posterior growth rate is unchanged between the two strains.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the measurement data.

claim: Spry2 and Sostdc1 are downregulated in DUHi lower and upper molar samples.
source: Among all those DE genes, we identified two genes, Spry2 and Sostdc1 (also known as Ectodin), whose knock-out causes the formation of a premolar-like tooth (Ahn et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2011; Klein et al., 2006). Where it was specifically investigated, this premolar tooth was demonstrated to arise from R2 revival (Ahn et al., 2010; Klein et al., 2006; Peterkova et al., 2009). The downregulation of these two genes in DUHi lower and upper molar samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) could thus help the partial rescue of R2 bud in this strain.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, with citations to support the functional interpretation.

claim: The downregulation of Spry2 and Sostdc1 in DUHi could help the partial rescue of R2 bud in this strain.
source: The downregulation of these two genes in DUHi lower and upper molar samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) could thus help the partial rescue of R2 bud in this strain.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the gene expression data and known functions.

claim: For the BMP4 pathway, there were 20 genes in favor of weaker BMP4 activation in DUHi versus only 7 genes in favor of greater BMP4 activity.
source: For the BMP4 pathway, there were 20 genes in favor of weaker BMP4 activation in DUHi (e.g. summing activated targets that are upregulated with repressed targets that are downregulated, see Appendix 2 for more detail and Figure 4N) versus only 7 genes in favor of greater BMP4 activity (e.g. summing activated targets that are downregulated with repressed targets that are upregulated).
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The two-fold difference in BMP4 pathway target genes is significant (p=0.01 in a χ2 test).
source: This two-fold difference is significant (p=0.01 in a χ2 test).
evidence: This statistical finding is stated in the text.

claim: For the Wnt pathway, there is no trend with 23 genes in favor of weaker Wnt activity in DUHi and 20 genes in favor of greater Wnt activity.
source: For the Wnt pathway, we found no trend with 23 genes in favor of weaker Wnt activity in DUHi and 20 genes in favor of greater Wnt activity (Figure 4N).
evidence: This quantitative comparison is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Four feedback inhibitors of the Wnt pathway are upregulated in DUHi mice (Axin2, Kremen1, Osr2, Sfrp2).
source: Intriguingly, this included 4 feedback inhibitors of the Wnt pathway upregulated in DUHi mice (Axin2, Kremen1, Osr2; Sfrp2) and 3 feedback inhibitors downregulated in DUHi (Dkk1, Wif1, Sostdc1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text.

claim: Three feedback inhibitors of the Wnt pathway are downregulated in DUHi (Dkk1, Wif1, Sostdc1).
source: Intriguingly, this included 4 feedback inhibitors of the Wnt pathway upregulated in DUHi mice (Axin2, Kremen1, Osr2; Sfrp2) and 3 feedback inhibitors downregulated in DUHi (Dkk1, Wif1, Sostdc1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text.

claim: Finding major regulators of Wnt activity differentially expressed suggests that Wnt activity differs between FVB and DUHi.
source: Finding these major regulators of Wnt activity in tooth development differentially expressed suggests that Wnt activity differs between FVB and DUHi, although we cannot orient it as for the BMP pathway.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the gene expression data.

claim: Culturing upper molars ex vivo results in a partial rescue of the upper R2 bud, which occurs much more frequently in DUHi than in FVB mice (Fisher exact test; p=0.015).
source: Culturing upper molars, we have occasionally observed such a rescue of the upper R2 bud which starts to form an independent tooth cap (Figure 4M). This occurred much more frequently in DUHi than in FVB mice (Figure 4K–M; Fisher exact test; p=0.015).
evidence: This experimental finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4, with statistical support.

claim: The activation-inhibition balance differs between DUHi and FVB strains.
source: We concluded that the activation-inhibition balance differs between the two strains.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: R2 persisted longer in the upper than in the lower jaw in both strains (Fisher exact test, p=0.04).
source: In both strains, we found similar lower-upper jaw differences as seen in CD1 mice, namely 1) R2 persisted longer in the upper than in the lower jaw, as tested via a Fisher exact test on samples for which data were available for both upper and lower jaws of the same embryo (p=0.04).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: In the lower jaw only, the M1 Shh expression zone encompasses the zone of the R2 signaling center.
source: 2) The M1 Shh expression zone increased in size in upper as in lower jaw, but in the lower jaw only it encompassed the zone of the R2 signaling center (compare Figure 2Q–T and Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q–T).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The spatio-temporal dynamics and fate of the R2 signaling center relative to M1 signaling center differs between the two jaws, regardless of difference in activation-inhibition mechanisms between strains.
source: Thus, the spatio-temporal dynamics and fate of the R2 signaling center relative to M1 signaling center differs between the two jaws, regardless of difference in activation-inhibition mechanisms between strains.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative observations.

claim: The difference between lower and upper jaw developmental systems can be considered a conserved developmental property.
source: This can be considered a conserved developmental property of the lower and upper developmental systems.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the consistent differences observed.

claim: For upper molars treated during R2 signaling center activity, the anterior part of the tooth is marked at 17.5 dpc.
source: For upper molars treated during R2 signaling center activity, the anterior part of the tooth is marked at 17.5 dpc (Figure 5C).
evidence: This observation from lineage tracing is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The anterior region of the upper molar is unmarked when tamoxifen is applied later, during M1 signaling center activity only.
source: However, this anterior region is unmarked when tamoxifen is applied later, during M1 signaling center activity only (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This observation from lineage tracing is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The fate of the cell populations of R2 signaling center is the anterior region of the first upper molar.
source: Thus, the fate of the cell populations of R2 signaling center is the anterior region of the first upper molar.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage tracing experiments.

claim: In the first lower molar, the same region is stained in all three tamoxifen treatment conditions.
source: In the case of the first lower molar, the same region is stained in all three conditions (Figure 5F–H), consistent with R2 signaling center being overwritten by the mature M1 signaling center (Sadier et al., 2019).
evidence: This observation from lineage tracing is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5, with a citation to support the interpretation.

claim: In the lower molar, the R2 signaling center does not contribute specifically to the most anterior part.
source: Moreover, the anterior part of the first molar is unstained. Thus, in the lower molar, the R2 signaling center does not contribute specifically to the most anterior part.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: A change in R2 size and R2-M1 centers distance in DUHi upper jaw will directly elongate the anterior part of the upper M1.
source: From these results, we can deduce that a change in R2 size and R2-M1 centers distance, as seen in DUHi upper jaw, will directly elongate the anterior part of the upper M1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as a deduction from the lineage tracing results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The more modest change seen in the DUHi lower jaw may elongate the M1, but not specifically from its anterior part.
source: In contrast, the more modest change seen in the DUHi lower jaw may elongate the M1, but not specifically from its anterior part (compare Figure 5I with Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is stated as a deduction from the lineage tracing results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Intrinsic differences between lower and upper M1 developmental systems are responsible for their different reactions to variations in activation-inhibition mechanisms.
source: We conclude that intrinsic differences between lower and upper M1 developmental systems are responsible for their different reactions: marked anterior elongation in the upper molar and a more discrete and isometric elongation of the lower molar (see Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative developmental and lineage tracing data.

claim: DUHi samples display different states for similar embryonic age.
source: A brief examination revealed that DUHi samples display different states for similar embryonic age (Figure 3 and S7).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: DUHi upper molars have greater developmental variation than FVB upper molars (Wilcoxon test, p<0.001).
source: Our method yielded a highly significant result in both cases, (p<0.001 for Wilcoxon tests) where DUHi was more variable than FVB in both cases.
evidence: This statistical finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: DUHi lower molars have greater developmental variation than FVB lower molars (Wilcoxon test, p<0.001).
source: Our method yielded a highly significant result in both cases, (p<0.001 for Wilcoxon tests) where DUHi was more variable than FVB in both cases.
evidence: This statistical finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Not only do the developmental trajectories of DUHi and FVB strains differ from one another, but the degree of variation within each strain is not equivalent.
source: Therefore, not only do the developmental trajectories of these two strains differ from one another, but the degree of variation within each strain is not equivalent.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the developmental variation analysis.

claim: There is a small peak in developmental variation between computed age 14–15 cdpc/weight: 150–250 mg in both upper and lower molars.
source: A similar pattern is seen in both upper and lower molars, whereby there is a small peak in developmental variation between computed age 14–15 cdpc/weight: 150–250 mg, followed by a decrease in developmental variation.
evidence: This pattern is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peak in developmental variation is considerably greater, in both duration and magnitude, in DUHi than FVB samples.
source: This peak is considerably greater, in both duration and magnitude, in DUHi than FVB samples.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the upper molars, the peak in developmental variation corresponds to the period when two signaling centers coexist and the M1 signaling center expands (14.5–14.75 cdpc/Weight: 200–220 mg).
source: In the upper molars, it corresponds to the period when two signaling centers coexist and the M1 signaling center expands (14.5–14.75 cdpc/Weight: 200–220 mg, Figure 6B).
evidence: This temporal correspondence is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: DUHi mice show greater variation in upper molar length than FVB (p=0.095), to an extent comparable to the outbred CD1 mice.
source: Although they are also an inbred strain, DUHi mice show greater variation in upper molar length than FVB (p=0.095), to an extent comparable to the outbred CD1 mice.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The variation in DUHi upper molar length is consistent with the large degree of variation in R2/M1 development in DUHi embryonic upper jaws.
source: The variation in DUHi upper molar length is consistent with the large degree of variation in R2/M1 development in DUHi embryonic upper jaws.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation connecting developmental and adult variation.

claim: The variation in length is specific to the upper molars: In the lower molars, DUHi individuals show little variation in length, albeit large variation in width.
source: Consistent with the developmental data, this variation in length is specific to the upper molars: In the lower molars, DUHi individuals show little variation in length, albeit large variation in width (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inter-strain variation was used as a proxy for natural variation.
source: We have used inter-strain variation as a proxy for natural variation.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological choice in the discussion.

claim: The morphological variation between FVB and DUHi mice recapitulates the morphological variation in the Mus genus and beyond.
source: We think this choice is relevant for three reasons: 1) We show that the morphological variation between FVB and DUHi mice recapitulates the morphological variation in the Mus genus and beyond
evidence: This is stated as justification for the choice of strains.

claim: The DUHi mice recapitulate the correlation between anterior elongation and large body size seen in natural populations of Mus musculus domesticus.
source: 2) The DUHi mice are a product of artificial selection in the lab for large body size, starting from six different mouse strains (Bünger and Herrendörfer, 1994; Bünger et al., 1982). It thus also recapitulates the correlation between anterior elongation and large body size seen in natural populations of Mus musculus domesticus (Renaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as justification for the choice of strains, with citations.

claim: Lab mice were derived from a mix of several mouse subspecies (Mus musculus domesticus, Mus musculus musculus, Mus musculus castaneus).
source: 3) Lab mice were derived from a mix of several mouse subspecies (Mus musculus domesticus, Mus musculusmusculus, Mus musculus castaneus).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about lab mice.

claim: The anterior development of the first upper molar varies between DUHi and FVB strains.
source: We show that the anterior development of the first upper molar varies between DUHi and FVB strains.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: In DUHi mice compared to FVB mice, there is a larger size of R2 rudimentary bud, longer persistence of its signaling center, a posteriorisation of the M1 signaling center, a marked tendency for R2 to individualise in culture, and differences in gene expression.
source: We show inter-related differences such as, in DUHi mice compared to FVB mice, the larger size of R2 rudimentary bud, the longer persistence of its signaling center, a posteriorisation of the M1 signaling center, a marked tendency for R2 to individualise in culture and differences in gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: A similar tendency to DUHi, although less marked, is seen in the DUHi lower molar.
source: A similar tendency, although less marked, is seen in the DUHi lower molar.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: These two strains differ in the settings of the activation-inhibition mechanisms patterning the tooth signaling centers.
source: Collectively, these results show that these two strains differ in the settings of the activation-inhibition mechanisms patterning the tooth signaling centers.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the collective findings.

claim: The balance of activation-inhibition is shifted for the BMP4 pathway, with overall weaker BMP4 activity in DUHi mice.
source: We have indications that the balance is shifted for the BMP4 pathway, with the expression levels of BMP4 targets suggesting overall weaker BMP4 activity in DUHi mice, which would mean reduced activation in DUHi mice (activation is taken here in a broad sense, and may include different mechanisms, as suggested in the results).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the gene expression data.

claim: Reduced activation in culture or in the Edar mutant favors the R2 bud in its competition with the M1 signaling center and thereby tends to rescue it.
source: Although R2 partial rescue in a context of reduced activation may appear counter-intuitive at first glance, it is in line with our recent study showing that reduced activation in culture or in the Edar mutant favors the R2 bud in its competition with the M1 signaling center and thereby tends to rescue it Sadier et al. (2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the interpretation.

claim: The narrow morphology of DUHi (lower and upper) molars as compared with the broad, massive morphology of FVB molars is consistent with decreased levels of activation in this strain.
source: We note that the narrow morphology of DUHi (lower and upper) molars as compared with the broad, massive morphology of FVB molars is also consistent with decreased levels of activation in this strain.
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with the activation-inhibition interpretation.

claim: In Orkney house mouse populations, the presence of the anterior cusp was associated with a decrease in overall cusp complexity, consistent with overall decreased level of activation.
source: We have noticed in a study of Orkney house mouse populations that the presence of the anterior cusp was associated with a decrease in overall cusp complexity, again consistent with overall decreased level of activation (Renaud et al., 2018).
evidence: This observation is stated with a citation.

claim: The two lines of least resistance seen in murine rodents (anterior elongation of the upper molar and variation in shape seen in both molars) are developmentally coupled by a common setting of the activation/inhibition balance.
source: In conclusion, our results thus suggest that the two lines of least resistance seen in murine rodents: the anterior elongation of the upper molar, and the variation in shape seen in both molars are developmentally coupled by a common setting of the activation/inhibition balance.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the collective findings.

claim: The R2 signaling center is intrinsically stronger in the upper jaw.
source: First, we show that the R2 signaling center is intrinsically stronger in the upper jaw, remains independent of the M1 signaling center and contributes to the anterior part (cervical loop) of upper M1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: The R2 signaling center remains independent of the M1 signaling center in the upper jaw.
source: First, we show that the R2 signaling center is intrinsically stronger in the upper jaw, remains independent of the M1 signaling center and contributes to the anterior part (cervical loop) of upper M1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: The R2 signaling center contributes to the anterior part (cervical loop) of upper M1.
source: First, we show that the R2 signaling center is intrinsically stronger in the upper jaw, remains independent of the M1 signaling center and contributes to the anterior part (cervical loop) of upper M1.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: In the lower jaw, R2 bud is smaller, included in the mature M1 signaling center (pEK), and R2 signaling center cells do not contribute to the anterior cervical loop, but to a more central part of the molar.
source: This is contrasted with the lower jaw, where R2 bud is smaller, included in the mature M1 signaling center (so-called pEK) and R2 signaling center cells do not contribute to the anterior cervical loop, but to a more central part of the molar.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: Subtle variations in activation-inhibition mechanisms that would affect R2 signaling center could specifically impact the anterior part of the upper M1 only.
source: As a consequence, subtle variations in activation-inhibition mechanisms that would affect R2 signaling center could specifically impact the anterior part of the upper M1 only, whereas this effect could be either buffered in the lower M1 or spread on the whole tooth (DUHi lower M1 are longer than FVB).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative developmental findings.

claim: Upper molar development appears to be inherently more variable than lower molar development.
source: Secondly, upper molar development appears to be inherently more variable than lower molar development.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: DUHi and FVB mice are more different in terms of upper molar development than they are in terms of lower molar development.
source: DUHi and FVB mice are more different in terms of upper molar development than they are in terms of lower molar development; variation in R2 signaling center persistence, in anterior region size and M1 positioning are all stronger for upper than lower molars.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: The intrinsic variability of the upper molar is apparent in the phenotypic variability of the DUHi mice.
source: This intrinsic variability of the upper molar is also apparent in the phenotypic variability of the DUHi mice.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation connecting developmental and adult variation.

claim: Although DUHi mice are inbred, the upper molar is much more variable in length.
source: Although these mice are inbred, the upper molar is much more variable in length and this is correlated, again, with greater developmental variability in upper R2 signaling center (we note, however, that the lower M1 of DUHi mice is highly variable in width, Figure 6—figure supplement 1: this might indicate that the lower M1 also reacts to changes in R2, albeit very differently).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The variation in upper molar length in DUHi mice is correlated with greater developmental variability in upper R2 signaling center.
source: Although these mice are inbred, the upper molar is much more variable in length and this is correlated, again, with greater developmental variability in upper R2 signaling center (we note, however, that the lower M1 of DUHi mice is highly variable in width, Figure 6—figure supplement 1: this might indicate that the lower M1 also reacts to changes in R2, albeit very differently).
evidence: This correlation is stated in the text.

claim: Upper molar development is intrinsically unstable, especially when the tuning of activation-inhibition parameters comes in the 'DUHi range'.
source: This suggests that upper molar development is intrinsically unstable, especially when the tuning of activation-inhibition parameters comes in the 'DUHi range'.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the variability findings.

claim: The study uncovered the basis for an evolutionary line of least resistance in murine rodents, leading to repeated morphological evolution of the first upper molar in mice.
source: We thus uncovered the basis for an evolutionary line of evolutionary least resistance in murine rodents, leading to repeated morphological evolution of the first upper molar in mice.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the collective findings.

claim: The work identifies strong variation in early tooth development between strains (morphology of the tooth germ and dynamics of signaling centers) in tandem with relatively mild variation in adult phenotype.
source: Here, our work identifies strong variation in early tooth development between strains (morphology of the tooth germ and dynamics of signaling centers) in tandem with relatively mild variation in adult phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings in the discussion.

claim: Heterozygotes may have important differences in early development, making their use as controls unreliable in systems like that observed in this study.
source: In systems like that observed here, heterozygotes may have important differences in early development, making their use as controls unreliable.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the findings for experimental practices.

claim: R2 is much less transient and discrete in the CD1 strain, where R2 was first identified, than in FVB.
source: In this context, it is interesting that the recognition of R2 vestigial bud presence in mouse molar development was a matter of debate for several years, and R2 is much less transient and discrete in the CD1 strain, where R2 was first identified, than in FVB, in which much heavier sampling is needed to catch the short developmental window when it is present.
evidence: This observation is stated as an example of strain differences affecting research.
